meaning: Whatever the agency runs on a route: a van, a shuttle, a minibus or a car. The apps never call it by one of those.
A line of service, such as route 7 or Ngong Road, as the agency's timetable names it.
One scheduled journey of a route at a set time, which the driver picks before starting.
The driver's journey in the app, from starting it to ending it, while the app sends the vehicle's position.
A place on the route where riders get on and off.
The chain of runs one vehicle drives in a day.
The transit operator that runs the service, and the server the drivers sign in to.
The person at the agency who watches the vehicles and answers drivers.
One position the app sends to the server. The trip bar counts them.
Enter the email address and password the agency gave the driver.
Leave the account so the next driver can sign in on the same phone.
The agency's computer the app sends reports to, named by its web address.
Within the agency's window around the timetable: by default from 1 minute early to 5 minutes late.
Behind the timetable.
Ahead of the timetable. Riders may miss the vehicle.
Away from the route's line on the map.
Far from the timetable, so the driver may have picked the wrong run.
The phone's position, which the app needs permission to read.
The phone setting that gives the exact position rather than an area.
The button that starts sending reports for the picked run.
The button that stops sending reports and finishes the trip.
Carry on reporting a trip that stopped, for example after the phone restarted.
The link or QR code from the agency that fills in the server's address.
The open-source project the apps are part of.
The apps' name.
Apple's in-car screen.
Apple's phone.
Google's phone software.
The satellite positioning the phone uses.
